title: Oregon Blew Up a Dead Whale. It Rained Blubber. #shorts
description:
Case 041. On 12 November 1970 a dead whale, about 45 feet long and some 8 tons, lay on the beach at Florence, Oregon. The Oregon State Highway Division, with assistant district engineer George Thornton in charge, packed twenty 50-pound cases of dynamite (half a ton) against it, expecting the blast to leave pieces small enough for seagulls and other scavengers to clean up. Spectators were moved back into the dunes. Walter Umenhofer, who had explosives training from the military, said it was far too much and watched from further back than the rest of the crowd. The blast threw a column of sand and whale into the air; blubber sailed over the spectators and people ran for their cars. About a quarter of a mile away, a slab of blubber crushed the roof of the new car Umenhofer had bought days earlier in a "whale of a deal" sales promotion; the state's insurer paid him the car's full value. Nobody was hit. Highway crews cleaned up what was left, and Thornton told the local paper it "went just exactly right". In 2020 the people of Florence voted to name a new park Exploding Whale Memorial Park. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The whale was already dead; nobody was hurt. The cars, cases, bulldozer and dealer's forecourt are generic low-poly shapes with no makes, logos or brand names, and nobody's likeness is attempted. The only words on screen are the documented sales slogan and the park's name. Staging details such as the look of the beach, the crates, the car, the dealer's forecourt, the park and the sign, who stood where, and everything Rook does are reconstruction, not record. Narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro).

experiments.E1_E2: spine v2: Rook is already on the dune ridge in shot 5 and doubts it in one line of 1.27 s ('Raining whale? Not a chance.') with the column still climbing behind him; no office. The story runs forward from the blast (the rain, the run for the cars) and steps back only once, for the plan, because the plan is what raises the stakes. Date, place and names are on-screen labels (12 NOV 1970, FLORENCE, OREGON, WALTER UMENHOFER, GEORGE THORNTON).
experiments.E3: The batch brief's ten Shorts are all made, so this Short is outside it. It opens on the subject close (the dead whale's flank and the stacked cases, low and near) and the blast lands 0.22 s in, rather than on a person's face.
experiments.E7: hook_text THEY BLEW UP / A WHALE.
experiments.E8: tail 0.4 s; the last line ('Because one day in Oregon,') runs into the first ('they blew up a dead whale...'), and the last shot settles into the opening framing with the whale whole, so the loop restarts on the blast.
experiments.tone: First Short from the owner's funny-cases list. The jokes are on the absurd plan, the warning and the car; the whale was already dead and nobody was hurt, so Rook can stay dry and amused to the end.
experiments.rook_action: Detective actions in the story world: he walks the stack tapping and counting the cases (10), and he runs a tape measure along the slab on the crushed roof (20). Mannerisms: hat brim low (5), hat hop (5, 10), magnifying glass and raised brow (16), beak pinch against the smell (20, 24), caw-laugh (22), hat brim dropping over his eyes (27), hat off to the sign (28), pocketing a shiny shell (30).

sound_plan.first_frame: Near-silence under the hook title, then a 'hit' and a 'boom' at 0.2 s of the first shot as the beach erupts (the gate needs an impact in the first second; here it is the story's own sound), then a crash.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense for Rook's line, action for the rain, calm for the plan, tense for the warning, action for the car, wonder for the 'whale of a deal' flashback, tense for the clean-up, triumph for the payoff, end.
sound_plan.effects: One to three cues a shot, each tied to something visible: whooshes for lumps in the air, splashes for lumps landing in sand, clunks for the cases, ticks for Rook's counting, gulls for the gull, a crash and a clunk for the roof, a gasp for the owner, a sputter for the bulldozer.
sound_plan.hush: Shot 25 (the engineer at the edge of the hole turns to us): the music drops out for the breath before 'He said it went just exactly right.'
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; measured in the local rehearsal, not listened to.

source_notes: Read for this run on 19 Nov 2026 through a fetch tool: Wikipedia ('Exploding whale'); the Eugene Register-Guard of 13 Nov 1970 ('When they blow up a whale, they really blow it up!', Larry Bacon, p. 1A) and 23 Nov 1970 ('Flying blubber claim paid', p. 3B), both as transcribed on theexplodingwhale.com; Salem Reporter ('How Salem newspapers covered Oregon's exploding whale catastrophe', quoting AP and UPI reports of 1970); Jalopnik (Lalita Chemello, 16 Mar 2022, from a 2008 Register-Guard interview with the car's owner); Live Science (Mindy Weisberger, 18 Jun 2020); Offbeat Oregon (Finn J.D. John, 19 Oct 2008). Every narrated fact and every label is on at least two of them. Date 12 Nov 1970, Florence, Oregon: Wikipedia, Salem Reporter, Live Science, Register-Guard. Whale about 45 ft and some 8 tons: Wikipedia, Live Science, Register-Guard (45 ft), Salem Reporter (eight tons). It was already dead: all. Twenty cases of dynamite, half a ton: Register-Guard ('twenty 50-pound cases', 1,000 lb), Salem Reporter ('20 cases'), Wikipedia ('one-half short ton'), Live Science ('half-ton'), Offbeat Oregon. The plan, pieces small enough for seagulls and scavengers: Register-Guard (seagulls), Wikipedia ('scavenger animals'), Live Science ('scavenging birds and crabs'). Crowd moved back into the dunes: Register-Guard; blubber sailed over the spectators: Salem Reporter (AP), Register-Guard; people ran for their cars: Register-Guard ('sending many in the crowd to their cars'; the narration says 'people', not 'everyone') and Salem Reporter (KATU's 'run for survival'). Walter Umenhofer knew explosives from the military and warned it was too much: Offbeat Oregon (explosives training from his Second World War service, tried to warn Thornton and was brushed off), Wikipedia (a military veteran with explosives training warned that twenty cases was far too much; advice ignored), Register-Guard 23 Nov (his demolitions experience; 'improperly placed and overloaded'), Jalopnik ('That's gonna kill someone'). He watched from further back: Register-Guard 23 Nov, Offbeat Oregon. Spelling Umenhofer: Register-Guard 1970, Jalopnik, Offbeat Oregon (Salem Reporter has Unenhofer). A slab crushed the roof of his car about a quarter of a mile away: Salem Reporter (AP, 'caved in the roof', 'a quarter mile away'), Live Science ('about a quarter-mile', 'crushing the roof'), Register-Guard, Jalopnik; Offbeat Oregon says 450 yards. The car was new, bought days earlier in a 'whale of a deal' promotion: Wikipedia ('Get a Whale of a Deal' promotion, days before), Offbeat Oregon ('Get a Whale of a Deal on a New Oldsmobile', days earlier), Jalopnik (the dealer's motto, 'just bought'). The state's insurer paid the car's full value (description only): Register-Guard 23 Nov, Salem Reporter, Jalopnik. Nobody was hit: Register-Guard 13 Nov ('No one was hit'), Jalopnik ('no one was hurt'). Road crews cleaned up the rest: Register-Guard (a bulldozer moved in to bury the larger chunks), Wikipedia (left for Highway Division workers to clear away). George Thornton, assistant district engineer, in charge: Register-Guard, Salem Reporter, Wikipedia, Offbeat Oregon. 'It went just exactly right': Register-Guard 13 Nov, Wikipedia, Offbeat Oregon. Park named Exploding Whale Memorial Park in 2020 by a community vote (439 of 856 votes): Live Science, Wikipedia. Kept out because single-sourced or disputed: whether the seagulls came afterwards (only Wikipedia, citing the KATU report); how much of the whale was left (Wikipedia: most of it; Register-Guard: only the tail was recognisable), so the narration says only 'the rest'; the species (sperm whale per Wikipedia and Live Science, gray whale per Salem Reporter), so the model is a generic whale; the car's make, model and year (1969 Oldsmobile, 1970 Oldsmobile 98, Oldsmobile 88 Regency), so it is a generic gold sedan with no badge; the size of the chunk (three feet square vs a small truck tyre); the 800-foot throw; who pushed the plunger; every quotation except Thornton's. The KATU film and its narration, and the Dave Barry column, are not used or quoted. Staging that is not fact: the look of the beach, the dunes, the lot, the cases and the blasting machine; the workmen; who stood where; the gold colour of the car; the dealer's forecourt, its banner layout and the handing over of the keys; the park's look and the sign's design; the shell; everything Rook does.

authoring.run: scheduled short run, 19 Nov 2026; the first slate idea, case 040, was claimed by a parallel run about a minute earlier, so this run took case 041

quality_gate.method: One run, eight review rounds. Rounds 1 to 3: low-res contact sheets of all 31 shots (one frame each) and targeted stills at two moments of every shot. Found and fixed: the sea sitting exactly level with the sand (a black band across every horizon, and half the blasting-machine shot black); the dune mesh built facing down; a driftwood log right in front of the opening camera; the cases reading as a brick wall (now pale wooden cases with slats and blank labels); lumps of blubber reading as rocks (now pale fat with a grey cap of skin); workmen and the engineer out of frame in the cases shot; the crowd too small in the rain shot; the man walking away hidden behind the dune crest; the magnifying glass held above Rook's hat; the clipboard covering the engineer's face and his thumbs-up reading as a head scratch; Rook out of frame at the park; a white flash sphere filling the opening frames (removed; the overlay draws the flash, and the light was cut by four fifths). Round 4: first full rehearsal (216x384, 4 samples, 12 fps, all 3D frames) composited with captions, labels, overlays and sound: the gate failed on six static stretches. Fixed in the film, never in the gate: wind ripples, pebbles, shells, grass and gravel on the ground so moving cameras have something to read, and real camera moves and acting in the gull, wire, warning, walk-back, magnifier, car, forecourt, bulldozer, engineer and park shots. Round 5: second rehearsal, one static stretch left (the engineer close-up), so he now sweeps an arm at the mess before the nod and the bulldozer rolls across behind him; gate PASS. Round 6: eight stills at 720x1280 with production samples (opening, Rook on the ridge, the crushed roof, his face, the engineer, the park, the sign-off, the forecourt): no blown-out or crushed frame, faces read at 270x480. Round 7: the whale rebuilt as one long tapering body (the three overlapping ellipsoids read as boulders) and the opening reframed to show the whole flank with the cases; two narration lines tightened to what two sources say ('People ran', not 'Everyone ran'; 'from the military', not 'from the war'). Round 8: third rehearsal from scratch with the new voice track: local gate PASS: 31 shots, mean 1.35 s, longest 2.15 s, Rook acting in 12 of 31 shots (39%), -14.4 LUFS, peak -1.2 dBFS, voice 17.9 dB over the bed, closest match to any earlier episode 0.65 (shot 18 against r006-wisnierska; the limit is 0.93). Duration 41.7 s. The longest label was shortened afterwards (GEORGE THORNTON); that changes only the overlay. The cloud render runs the real gate at 720x1280 and 60 fps.
quality_gate.gate_history: Rehearsal 1 failed on six static stretches (12.0-14.2, 15.8-19.2, 23.7-26.8, 29.7-31.5, 32.0-33.8 and 35.3-39.0 s): flat sand and sky gave moving cameras nothing to read. Rehearsal 2 failed on one (32.2-33.8 s, the engineer close-up). Rehearsal 2 with the fix and rehearsal 3 passed.
quality_gate.checked: Every 3D kind in the storyboard exists in world3d.SHOTS3D (checked by script); there are no flat inserts; HOST lists the 12 kinds in which Rook is placed; blast_close is the only kind used twice (first and last shot, for the loop) and no kind repeats back to back. First shot 1.0 s with the hit and boom at 0.2 s of it. The doubt line is 1.27 s and is spoken on the ridge with the column behind Rook. Re-hook (the slab lands on the car of the one man who warned them) starts at 19.6 s of 41.7 s (47%). One hush shot (25). Tail 0.4 s; the last shot settles into the opening framing. On-screen dates, names and figures (CASE 041, 12 NOV 1970, FLORENCE, OREGON, 20 CASES OF DYNAMITE, HALF A TON, WALTER UMENHOFER, KNEW EXPLOSIVES, A QUARTER MILE AWAY, GEORGE THORNTON, FLORENCE, 2020, the banner A WHALE OF A DEAL! and the sign EXPLODING WHALE MEMORIAL PARK) checked against the sources.
quality_gate.not_met: Not watched or listened to in real time: the review was 4-frames-per-second sheets of the whole composited rehearsal plus the gate's audio measurements. Loudness range was not measured separately. The three random one-second spot checks at full resolution were done as single full-resolution stills, not full one-second ranges. Labels pop in at 1.6 times their size for their first 0.2 s (engine behaviour), so long labels touch the frame edge for a few frames.

review.weakest: The sand column and the lumps are faceted spheres, so the blast reads stylised and partly like a heap of boulders. The whale is a smooth grey body that leans on the hook title to read as a whale in the first frame. People in the wide shots (the crowd on the ridge, the run to the lot, the forecourt) are small on a phone. The humans are block figures with simple faces. Daylight is flat sun and sky with no dramatic light. Narration and sound were measured, not heard.
